hero.title: AI recommends Italy to people deciding where to go. Not all of Italy.
hero.lead: A traveller asks “where should I go to the seaside in Italy”. They get five names, not fifty links. We measure who makes those five, across a hundred territories and two thousand hotels.

score.label: AI Visibility Score
score.stability-help: How much the score moved from one question to the next within the same month. If it moves little, you can count on it.

comparative.name: How often it's recommended
comparative.help: Someone asks an AI where to go in Italy for this kind of holiday. Does this territory show up in the answer? And in which position?

technical.name: Whether they can read it
technical.help: Do the programs that read websites for AI find the door open or shut? An AI won't recommend what it was never allowed to read.

factors.lead: Four factors, different weights. The score is built here, and here is where you see what it loses.

engines.lead: ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity don't read the same sources and don't reward the same things. A single mark would hide exactly the difference worth knowing.

entities.lead: The places that are genuinely here. We count how many each assistant names: it's the most concrete way to tell whether it knows the territory or is guessing.

funnel.title: Where the territory loses ground
funnel.lead: A trip is decided in three moments: first you dream, then you plan, finally you book. A territory can be strong in the dream and vanish when it's time to choose where to sleep.

answers.lead: So far we've counted mentions. This is the answer they land in: the text a traveller actually reads, with the destination's name in it — or without.

destination.cta-body: This page is one piece of a bigger picture. Compare this territory with another, look at the questions the score comes from, or read how we calculate it.

national.title: Italy in one number
national.lead: The average across the hundred territories we follow, and how differently the three assistants see it.
national.categories-lead: Twenty territories per category. Comparing only means something between comparable things: a village of eight hundred people isn't competing with Rome.
national.crawl-lead: How many Italian travel websites block each reading program. Every block is a decision, almost always taken without knowing it was one.

methodology.title: How we calculate the score
methodology.lead: The formula is public, and this page reads it from the code that applies it. They cannot tell two different stories.
methodology.engines-title: One general score, one per assistant
methodology.engines-body: The general one is the plain average of the three. No hidden weighting between assistants: if ChatGPT counted more than Perplexity, that would be our opinion dressed up as a measurement.
methodology.runs-body: The same question asked twice of the same model gives two different answers. One question isn't data, it's an anecdote. Every month we repeat everything five times per assistant and publish the average with how much it moved: that ± next to the number is the difference between an observatory and a screenshot.
methodology.technical-title: Why it matters whether a site lets itself be read
methodology.technical-body: An AI won't recommend what it couldn't read. Each assistant sends its own programs out to read websites: if a territory blocks ChatGPT's, its ChatGPT score drops. This isn't technical hygiene, it's visibility.
methodology.levels-body: In the first, the territory competes with the others in its category. In the second, we only check whether the AI knows it. They are two different things and deserve separate measurement: there are famous territories AI cannot describe, and small ones it describes beautifully.
methodology.data-body: At this stage the numbers are generated. The schema, the formula and the pages are final: when real runs replace the simulated dataset, not a line of this methodology changes.
methodology.formula-example: Illustrative example: numbers chosen to show how the four factors add up to the score, not any real territory's result.

assumptions.title: What we take for granted
assumptions.lead: The limits, before the results. An observatory that doesn't declare its assumptions isn't one.

items.title: The traveller has already chosen Italy
items.body: We don't measure Italy against Spain or Greece. We measure competition inside Italy: once the country is settled and the territory is still open.

items.title: We analyse three stages out of five
items.body: Dreaming, Planning and Booking are the stages where an AI answer can still move the decision. Experiencing and Sharing happen after booking: they matter for reputation, not acquisition, and are better measured elsewhere.

items.title: Two languages, not every market
items.body: Italian stands for domestic demand, English for international demand. German, French and Spanish are left out, and they are significant inbound markets for Italy. That's a real limit, and we state it here rather than let you infer it.

items.title: Prompts without personalisation
items.body: We query the models with no history, no account, no user geolocation. We measure the baseline answer, not the one a user with two years of conversations receives.

items.title: AI changes its mind
items.body: The same prompt gives different answers minutes apart. That's why every value is the average of five monthly runs per engine, published with its spread.

items.title: Twenty hotels are a sample
items.body: For each destination we follow twenty properties chosen for relevance and range. It isn't the territory's full hotel universe and doesn't pretend to be.

items.title: This phase's data is simulated
items.body: Scores, citations, crawler behaviour, volumes and CPC are generated to build and demonstrate the tool. Official and editorial domains are generated from the destination name rather than taken from real sites: publishing that an existing organisation blocks a crawler without having checked would simply be false.

rank.help: A bare position would promise a precision five measurements a month don't deliver. Next to it you'll find the range the territory genuinely sits in, and the band, which is the figure to rely on.
rank.tiers-lead: Between 38th and 41st place there is no measurable difference. Between one band and the next there is. Bands are the honest way to read this ranking.

demand.title: Demand scale
demand.help: How many monthly searches the questions we track here actually move. It tells you whether a ranking position is worth thousands of people or a few dozen.
demand.marginal-note: Mind the scale: this territory moves {n} searches a month across the queries we monitor. The 20-hotel ranking stays comparable with other destinations, but here a position is worth a few dozen searches, not thousands.

ui.share-section: Copy the link to this section
ui.related-lead: Same category or same themes: these are the territories it actually competes with.
ui.glossary-lead: Explained the way we'd explain them out loud, not the way a manual would write them.
ui.runs-lead: We measure once a month, repeating every question five times. Each point is an average; the bar says how much the answers moved within that month.

explain.score: A 0 to 100 mark for how often an AI names this territory when someone asks where to go. A hundred means it always comes up, first. Zero means that for the AI it doesn't exist.
explain.band: The number after the ± tells you how much the answer changed from one question to the next within the same month. The smaller it is, the more reliable the score.
explain.engines: Assistants don't draw on the same sources, so they don't give the same answers. If your territory does well on one and badly on another, the problem is specific and so is the fix.
explain.comparative: Picture someone asking an AI “where should I go to the seaside in Italy”. This number says how often this territory shows up in the answer, and in which position.
explain.internal: If someone asks “what is there to see here”, can the AI name real places, or does it stop at the two everybody knows? This measures how well it knows the place.
explain.sources: Where the AI gets its information when it talks about this territory. If it takes it from Booking rather than the official site, the destination is being described by someone who profits from it.
explain.technical: Can the programs that read websites on behalf of AI get in, or do they find the door shut? An AI cannot recommend what it was never allowed to read.
explain.entities: The things that are actually here. We check how many of them each assistant names: it's the most concrete way to tell whether it knows the place or is improvising.
explain.funnel: A trip is decided in three moments: first you dream, then you plan, finally you book. A destination can be strong in the dream and disappear when it's time to choose where to sleep.
explain.lang: People searching in Italian are almost always Italian travellers; people searching in English come from abroad. AI describes Italy differently to the two, and here you can see by how much.
explain.sites: The websites that talk about this territory, and whether AI programs can read them. A tick means the door is open, a cross means it's shut.
explain.hotels: The twenty properties we follow here. The score says how often each one gets named when someone asks where to stay in this area.
explain.queries: The questions people actually type, with how many times a month and what that click would cost to buy in advertising.
explain.prompts-comparative: The questions where this territory competes with the others in its category. If it doesn't appear in the answer, for whoever asked it doesn't exist.
explain.prompts-internal: Questions about this territory alone. Nothing to compete with here: this only shows whether the AI knows it.
explain.demand: How many monthly searches the questions we track here actually move. It tells you whether a ranking position is worth thousands of people or a few dozen.
explain.tier: Bands group territories that genuinely match each other. There's no measurable difference between #38 and #41; between one band and the next there is.
explain.runs: Every month we ask the same questions five times to each assistant. The answers change, so we publish the average and how much they moved.

data.demand-simulated: Simulated value: it doesn't come from a keyword research tool yet.
data.site-verified: Verified on {date}: domain reachable and operator identified.
data.site-generated: Domain generated from the destination name. Not a real website.
data.site-regional: No organisation holds a mandate for this territory alone: the body promoting it is the regional DMO.
data.chain-domain: Chain domain: who may read this site is decided by the group, not the individual hotel.
data.site-waf: Blocks automated checking. The site is there, the check isn't.

hotelsPage.title: The hotels

hotelsPage.meta-title: The Italian hotels AI names most
hotelsPage.meta-description: Two thousand properties followed across a hundred territories, measured on ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity: ranking, filters, site access.
hotelsPage.national-lead: The properties named most often when someone asks where to stay in Italy. The territory ranking matters more than this one: a hotel competes with what's next door, not with everything.
hotelsPage.by-destination-lead: That's the comparison that means something. Open a territory to see its twenty properties.
hotelsPage.real-lead: The ones that exist and that we checked: the domain responds and the page names them.
hotelsPage.generated-note: Positions not yet covered by real properties carry generated names, marked as demonstrative.

confidence-help.verified: The domain responds and the page names this property.
confidence-help.chain: It sits on a chain domain: it exists, but who may read that site is decided by the group.
confidence-help.guarded: The domain exists and refuses automated checks. The site is there, the proof that it's this hotel isn't.
confidence-help.listed: Present in the starting list, not rechecked in this round.
confidence-help.generated: A name generated to show how the tool works. Not an existing hotel.
confidence-help.registry-web: Listed in the regional accommodation registry, with a declared website.
confidence-help.registry: Listed in the regional accommodation registry. No website on record.

hotelsPage.page-title: The Italian hotels AI names most
hotelsPage.legend-rank: **Position** — where the property sits among all three hundred. It doesn't change when you filter: that's how you tell whether a hotel is strong nationally or only in its own territory.
hotelsPage.legend-score: **Score** — how often the property is named when someone asks where to stay, from 0 to 100. The ± is how much the answer moved within the same month.
hotelsPage.legend-presence: **How often it shows** — the proportion of answers the property appears in at least once. A high score with a low share means: when it shows up it shows up well, but it rarely shows up.
hotelsPage.legend-confidence: **The tag next to the name** — how much we know about its website. "Verified" means the domain responds and the page names this hotel; "Generated name" means the row is a demo.
